# Introduction 

The National Football League (NFL) has 14 official positions for players: 7 offensive, 5 defensive, and 2 special teams positions. One of the offensive positions is the quarterback (QB), whose primary role is to lead the offense on the field. ESPN provides a lot of data on NFL games and players, including the Total Quarterback Rating (QBR), a metric on a scale from 0 to 100 that estimates a quarterback's overall contribution to winning. Higher QBR values indicate better performance.

In this module, you will learn how to predict Total Quarterback Rating using game-level data from the 2025 NFL Regular season. To predict QBR, we will use stepwise regression, and you will have the option to complete the analysis in R, Python, or Julia. After selecting the best model with stepwise regression, we will use quantile analysis to see which quantile of quarterbacks (e.g. the top 10%, bottom 10%, etc.) are best explained by the selected model.

To complete the regression analysis, we will use the programming environment [Visual Studio Code (VS Code)](https://code.visualstudio.com/). VS Code is very popular both in academic and industry settings, making it a valuable tool to become familiar with. One of the biggest advantages of using VS Code is that it supports multiple programming languages within a single interface, allowing you to work in R, Python, or Julia without switching environments.  

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" title="Learning Objectives" appearance="minimal"}
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

1.  Perform stepwise regression in Julia, R, or Python.

2.  Perform quantile regression in Julia, R, or Python.

3.  Understand how to interpret the results of stepwise and quantile regression.

:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" title="Activity Length" appearance="minimal"}
This could be suitable for an out of class activity or an activity that takes up one class period.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" title="Methods" appearance="minimal"}
**Technology Requirement:**

This activity is designed to be completed in `Julia`, `R`, or `Python` using VS Code. 

No previous experience with regression or VS Code is required, but some familiarity with one of the programming languages is recommended.
:::

# Data

The `nfl_qbr.csv` dataset contains 540 rows, with each row representing a quarterback's performance in a game during the 2025 NFL regular season. The dataset includes 65 unique quarterbacks and contains passing, rushing, and sack statistics that describe each quarterback's weekly performance throughout the season.

Download Data: [nfl_qbr.csv](nfl_qbr.csv)

<details>
<summary><b>Variable Descriptions</b></summary>

| Variable              | Description |
|-----------------------|-------------|
| week                  | Week of the NFL Regular Season |
| player                | Full name of the quarterback in this game |
| qbr                   | ESPN Total Quarterback Rating (0-100) for the quarterback in this game |
| completions           | Number of passes the quarterback completed this game |
| attempts              | Number of passes the quarterback attempted this game |
| passing_yards         | Total yards gained through the quarterback's passing in this game |
| passing_tds           | Number of touchdown passes thrown by the quarterback in this game |
| passing_interceptions | Number of passes by the quarterback that were intercepted |
| sacks_suffered        | Number of times the quarterback was tackled behind the line of scrimmage this game |
| sack_yards_lost       | Total yards lost by the quarterback due to sacks this game |
| sack_fumbles          | Number of fumbles by the quarterback caused by sacks |
| sack_fumbles_lost     | Number of fumbles lost by the quarterback from sacks |
| passing_air_yards     | Total distance through the air of the quarterback's passes |
| passing_first_downs   | Number of first downs gained through the quarterback's passing |
| passing_epa           | Expected Points Added through the quarterback's passing plays |
| passing_cpoe          | Completion Percentage Over Expected for the quarterback's passes |
| pacr                  | Passing Air Conversion Ratio |
| carries               | Number of rushing attempts by the quarterback |
| rushing_yards         | Total rushing yards gained by the quarterback |
| rushing_tds           | Number of rushing touchdowns scored by the quarterback |
| rushing_fumbles       | Number of fumbles by the quarterback while rushing |
| rushing_fumbles_lost  | Number of rushing fumbles lost by the quarterback |
| rushing_first_downs   | Number of first downs gained through the quarterback's rushing |
| rushing_epa           | Expected Points Added through the quarterback's rushing plays |
| rest                  | Days of rest before the game for the quarterback's team |
| roof                  | Status of stadium's roof during this game (outdoors, dome, etc.) |
| surface               | Type of ground played on in this game |
| pct_total             | Percent of total points in this game scored by the quarterback's team |

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Data Source</b></summary>

The data was scraped from [ESPN's NFL statistics pages](https://www.espn.com/nfl/) using the R package [nflreadr](https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/). The dataset was created using the `nflreadr` functions `load_espn_qbr(2025, summary_type = "week")`, `load_schedules(2025)`, and `load_player_stats(2025, summary_level = "week")`, which provided weekly quarterback ratings, game information, and player performance statistics from the 2025 NFL regular season. 

After cleaning and joining the data sources, the final dataset included only quarterbacks who appeared in a regular season game during the 2025 NFL season. Each row in the dataset represents a single quarterback's performance for one game during a specific week of the season.

</details>

# Getting started in R

To start programming in R, you will need to install both [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and [R](https://cloud.r-project.org/).

Now, open R and use the following command to install the language server package:

```markdown
install.packages("languageserver")
```
Once that is complete, install the [R extension for VS Code](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=REditorSupport.r).

After you've installed everything needed to set up R in VS Code, we can create a project folder and get started.

Open VS Code and select File then select Open Folder. From there, you can either choose “New Folder” to create and name a new folder for this module, or, if that option is not available, navigate to the location on your computer where you would like the folder to be stored and create it there manually. Once the folder is created or selected, click “Select Folder” or “Open” on macOS to open it in VS Code. 

After the folder opens, it will become your workspace. You may be prompted with a pop-up asking whether you trust the authors of the files in this location. If so, select “Yes, I trust the authors.” Next, create a new file by selecting “New File” and choosing “R document.” 

At this point, if you have not already done so, download the dataset we will be using [(nfl_qbr.csv)](nfl_qbr.csv) and move it into your VS Code folder.

Reopen your R document. We are now ready for the final setup steps before running our regression analysis. Copy and paste the following code into your document to install the packages we will need and load in our dataset:

```markdown
install.packages("MASS")
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("quantreg")

library(tidyverse)
library(MASS)
library(quantreg)

nfl_qbr <- read_csv("nfl_qbr.csv") 
```

# Stepwise Regression

Stepwise regression helps find a useful combination of predictors for explaining a response variable by testing different combinations of predictors. For example, if we want to predict someone’s height, we might start with a dataset that includes height, age, sex, number of apples eaten a year, and full name. Stepwise regression looks at different combinations of the other variables and keeps the ones that help predict height the most.

The first step is to identify the variables that could reasonably help predict the response. For our dataset, the player statistics variables describe the quarterback’s performance in each game, and the game details variables describe the conditions surrounding the game that can affect performance. If you are not sure what a variable means, check the descriptions in the data section. If a variable seems like it might help, you can include it as a candidate predictor and let stepwise regression decide whether to keep it. A candidate predictor is a variable that is being considered as a candidate for being a predictor in our final model due to its potential to predict QBR.

It can be helpful to store the predictors in a vector so that you can easily add or remove variables while cleaning your data. For example, if a dataset included height, age, sex, apples_eaten_yearly, and name, you could store the variables you think might help predict height like this:

```markdown
predictors <- c("age", "sex", "apples_eaten_yearly")
```

Notice that full name was left out because it is only an identifier and does not help explain height. We also leave out height itself because that is the response variable we are trying to predict.

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 1: Prepare Predictors" icon = false}

Create a vector named predictors that contains the variables you want to use as explanatory variables in your stepwise regression model. Which variables from nfl_qbr should you include?

Remember, stepwise regression works best when it starts with a broad set of candidate predictors, since it will select the best combination for the final model. All variables are listed in the variable description tab under the data section above.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Solution</b></summary>

Most of the variables could help predict a quarterback’s performance, except for `player`, `qbr`, and `week`. We do not include `player` because it is only an identifier and would make the model depend too much on specific quarterbacks rather than patterns that generalize to new players. We do not include `week` because it is just a time label, and we do not include `qbr` because it is the response variable we are trying to predict.

```markdown
predictors <- c(
  "completions", "attempts", "passing_yards", "passing_tds", "passing_interceptions",
  "sacks_suffered", "sack_yards_lost", "sack_fumbles", "sack_fumbles_lost", 
  "passing_air_yards", "passing_first_downs", "passing_epa", "passing_cpoe",
  "pacr", "carries", "rushing_yards", "rushing_tds", 
  "rushing_fumbles", "rushing_fumbles_lost", "rushing_first_downs", "rushing_epa",
  "rest", "roof", "surface", "pct_total")
```
</details>
:::

Before we can use stepwise regression, we first fit a full linear model. A full linear model includes all of the candidate predictors we want to consider, so it gives us a starting point before stepwise regression begins removing or keeping variables.

If we made a full linear regression model to predict height using the imaginary data mentioned earlier, it would look something like this:

```markdown
full_mod <- lm(height ~ ., data = height_dataset[, c("height", predictors)])
```

We use height ~ . to tell the model to use all of the other variables from the data as predictors of height. Then we give the model only the variables we want it to use, including height and the predictors we selected.

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 2: Create a Full Model" icon = false}

Using qbr as the response variable, create a full linear regression model that includes all of the predictors in your predictors vector.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Solution</b></summary>

```markdown
full_mod <- lm(qbr ~ ., data = nfl_qbr[, c("qbr", predictors)])
```
</details>
:::

Now that we have fit a full linear regression model, we are ready to start stepwise regression. Stepwise regression is a way to find the best combination of predictors by adding or removing predictors one at a time. In forward selection, the model starts with no predictors and adds variables that improve the model. In backward elimination, the model starts with all predictors and removes variables that do not help much. In both directions, the model can add or remove predictors until it finds a better combination.

In this module, we use both forward and backward stepwise regression. That means the model starts with the full model, but it is also allowed to remove weak predictors and add back useful ones if needed.

For example, if we were predicting height from age, sex, and number of apples eaten a year, stepwise regression might start with all three variables, remove the number of apples eaten a year if it does not help, and keep age and sex if they improve the model. Using the `stepAIC()` function from the `MASS` package that we loaded in, that would look something like this:

```markdown
step_mod <- stepAIC(full_mod, direction = "both")
summary(step_mod)
```
The `stepAIC()` function searches for a smaller model with a lower AIC value. AIC is a number that helps compare models by balancing how well they fit the data with how simple they are, so a lower AIC usually means a better model. In this case, `direction = "both"`, means the function can try adding predictors, removing predictors, or doing both as it searches for the best model. 

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 3: Perform Stepwise Regression" icon = false}

Use stepwise regression with both forward and backward selection to choose the best combination of predictors from the full model. Then display the summary of the selected model. Which variables were kept?

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Solution</b></summary>

```markdown
step_mod <- stepAIC(full_mod, direction = "both")
summary(step_mod)
```
The variables that were kept in the best model picked by stepwise regression are: passing_yards, passing_tds, passing_interceptions, sack_yards_lost, passing_air_yards, passing_epa, passing_cpoe, rushing_first_downs, rushing_epa, surface, pct_total, and sack_fumbles.

</details>
:::

An important part of building a model is checking how well it performs. This helps us understand whether the model is doing a good job predicting the response variable. For stepwise regression, we can use the adjusted R-squared value in the model summary to measure how much of the variation in QBR is explained by the model. In general, values closer to 1 indicate a better fit to the data.

We can also use the model summary to identify which predictors are especially useful for explaining QBR. The `Pr(>|t|)` column contains p-values that measure whether each predictor is significantly related to the response variable. In the output, significant predictors are marked with asterisks (`*`). More asterisks indicate stronger statistical significance. The smaller the predictor's p-value is, the stronger it is associated with QBR in the model.

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 4: Describe Model Fit" icon = false}

Using the adjusted R-squared value, describe how well the model fits the data.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Example Answer</b></summary>

According to the model summary, the adjusted R-squared value was 0.7515. This means the model explains about 75.15% of the variation in QBR, which suggests that the model fits the data fairly well. Overall, the predictors selected by the stepwise regression procedure appear to capture many of the factors associated with quarterback performance.

</details>
:::

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 5: Identify Strongly Associated Predictors" icon = false}

Using the model summary for the stepwise regression model, identify which predictors in the stepwise model seem most strongly associated with QBR?

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Example Answer</b></summary>

The predictors in the stepwise model that seem the most strongly associated to QBR are `passing_tds`, `sack_yards_lost`, `passing_air_yards`, `passing_epa`, `passing_cpoe`, `rushing_first_downs`, and `rushing_epa` because they were all highly statistically significant, meaning they had very small p-values and strong relationships with QBR, denoted by three asterisks in the model summary.

</details>
:::

# Quantile Regression 

Quantile regression helps us study different parts of the response variable instead of only the average. A quantile is a point that splits the data into groups, like the 10th percentile, 25th percentile, or 50th percentile.

Similar to how we made a vector of predictors, we can make a vector of quantile values. For example:

```markdown
quantiles <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6)
```
This would represent the 20th, 40th, and 60th percentiles. A weekly QBR at the 20th percentile would be a higher QBR than 20% of all weekly QBR values and lower than 80% of them.

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 6: Set Quantiles" icon = false}

Create a vector named quantiles that includes the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Solution</b></summary>

```markdown
quantiles <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90)
```
</details>
:::

Now that we have a vector with all the quantiles we are interested in, we need to fit a quantile regression model for each value in the vector. We do this using the `rq()` function in the `quantreg` package for linear quantile regression and the `map()` function from `purrr` package in `tidyverse` to fit a model for each quantile. Using our imaginary height dataset, it would look like this:

```markdown
qr_models <- map(quantiles, ~ rq(height ~ age + sex, tau = .x, data = height_dataset))
```
We use `tau = .x` to set tau to every value in the list of quantiles we give it and we use the equation given to use by stepwise regression, so for this example age + sex, leaving out apples_eaten_yearly. 

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 7: Perform Quantile Regression" icon = false}

Using qbr as the response variable, fit a quantile regression model for each value in your quantiles vector. Use the predictors chosen by stepwise regression and store the models in a list called qr_models.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Solution</b></summary>

```markdown
qr_models <- map(quantiles, ~ rq(qbr ~ passing_yards + passing_tds + passing_interceptions + 
                                   sack_yards_lost + passing_air_yards + passing_epa + passing_cpoe +
                                   rushing_first_downs + rushing_epa + surface + pct_total + 
                                   sack_fumbles, tau = .x, data = nfl_qbr))
```
</details>
:::

Quantile regression doesn’t use the usual “squared error” from linear regression, so we can’t use regular R-squared to measure how well the model fits. Instead, we use something called pinball loss (also known as quantile loss) to see how close our predicted quantiles are to the real data. Pinball loss penalizes predicting QBR too high or too low differently depending on what quantile you are predicting for. For example, for the 10th percentile, being too high would be penalized more than being too low.

Here's an example of how to calculate it, copy and paste the following code into your R document to evaluate our selected model to see how accurately it predicts QBR for different quantiles:

```markdown
# Compute pinball loss for a quantile regression model
qr_pinball <- function(model, data, response, tau) {
  y <- data[[response]]
  y_hat <- predict(model, newdata = data)
  
  loss <- ifelse(y >= y_hat,
                 tau * (y - y_hat),
                 (1 - tau) * (y_hat - y))
  
  mean(loss)}

# Table of pinball loss for each quantile model
qr_pinball_table <- map_dfr(seq_along(qr_models), ~ {
  tibble(
    quantile = quantiles[.x],
    pinball_loss = qr_pinball(qr_models[[.x]], nfl_qbr, "qbr", quantiles[.x]))})
```

:::{.callout-note title="Exercise 9: Create a Visual" icon = false}

Using ggplot(), create a bar chart of pseudo R-squared by quantile. Put tau on the x-axis and r2 on the y-axis.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for Solution</b></summary>

```markdown
ggplot(pseudo_r2, aes(x = factor(tau), y = r2)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, fill = "darkgreen") +
  labs(
    x = "Tau",
    y = "Pseudo R^2",
    title = "Pseudo R^2 by Quantile") +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Garamond") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12, family = "Garamond"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, family = "Garamond"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, family = "Garamond"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12, family = "Garamond"),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12, family = "Garamond"))
```
</details>
:::
